title: Evanescent absorption spectroscopy of transition metal dichalcogenide materials using guided photoluminescence in Si$_3$N$_4$ photonic waveguides
authors: Victor Gonzalez-Morote, Marianna Sledzinska, Arkadiusz P. Gertych, Syed Hassan Abbas Jaffery, Mariusz Zdrojek, Daniel Navarro-Urrios
abstract: On-chip integration of two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) with photonic waveguides underpins a growing class of compact optoelectronic and sensing devices, whose performance depends on the optical absorption of the 2D material in this integrated environment. We demonstrate source-free, on-chip evanescent absorption spectroscopy of MoS$_2$ and WS$_2$ flakes integrated on Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguides, in which the broadband defect-related photoluminescence of the Si$_3$N$_4$ core itself acts as the internal probe. Light generated inside the core propagates under the TMD flake and is spectrally attenuated by evanescent interaction with the 2D material, and normalizing the transmitted spectrum to a reference waveguide without TMD yields the energy-dependent absorption response without any external illumination. The extracted guided absorption agrees with Raman and local micro-photoluminescence characterization and resolves differences between spatially uniform and non-uniform flakes. A complementary top-pumping scheme recovers guided WS$_2$ photoluminescence, whose spectral reshaping during propagation is quantitatively reproduced by the measured absorption. This source-free platform qualifies 2D materials in their integrated photonic environment and provides a direct route toward waveguide-integrated TMD photodetectors and sensors.
summary: The authors developed a novel, source-free technique to measure the optical absorption of 2D TMD materials integrated into $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ photonic waveguides. By monitoring how the waveguide's internal photoluminescence is spectrally attenuated by the overlying flake, they achieve an accurate, in situ measurement of excitonic absorption. This method is crucial for designing next-generation, high-performance on-chip optoelectronic devices.
main_problem: The primary goal is to characterize the optical absorption of 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) in their operational, integrated environment.
main_result: The study successfully demonstrates a source-free, on-chip spectroscopy technique that accurately measures energy-dependent TMD absorption by monitoring spectral attenuation of guided photoluminescence.
method: Evanescent absorption spectroscopy is performed by using the intrinsic defect-related photoluminescence from the $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ waveguide core as an internal probe source, which is then attenuated by the overlying TMD flake.
model_or_system: The system involves integrating TMD flakes ($	ext{MoS}_2$, $	ext{WS}_2$) onto a silicon nitride ($	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$) photonic waveguide. The measurement probes the interaction between the guided optical mode and the material's excitonic transitions.
key_observables: Energy-dependent absorption spectrum ($	ext{dB/cm}$), local photoluminescence ($\mu$-PL) spectra, and spectral reshaping of propagating PL.
important_parameters: Exciton binding energies (e.g., $\sim 1.83 	ext{ eV}$ for uniform $	ext{MoS}_2$), attenuation coefficients ($\alpha$ in $	ext{dB/cm}$), and flake coverage length ($L$).
main_assumptions: The measurement assumes the broadband defect-related PL dominates the signal, allowing normalization against a reference waveguide; furthermore, near resonances, reported attenuation values are conservative lower bounds.
figures_summary: Figures compare guided PL vs. local $\mu$-PL spectra, show extracted attenuation profiles, and illustrate the setup for both source-free spectroscopy and top-pumping excitation geometry.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for in situ characterization, details the source-free evanescent absorption method using internal PL, validates this technique by comparing results to local $\mu$-PL and Raman data, and concludes by positioning the platform for future photodetector development.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly relevant experimental methodology for quantum optics and open quantum systems research by characterizing material loss mechanisms (absorption) in solid-state devices that are critical for coupling light to quantum emitters or qubits.
